utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, representing the defence for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves. On behalf of my client, we have a request. Last week, the Trial Chamber allowed us to start the questioning of the witness and we are thankful for this, since on the 14th of this month there will be a continuation of the examination of our client in the Scheveningen prison and our client would like to waive his right because of this physical examination, and he would ask not to be present on the 13th and he agrees to waive his right to be present at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Olujic. I think your application will be granted. The accused has a right to determine whether he will be present or not. His condition is sufficient for him to stay away for his medical examination, but obviously you would know that, when it comes to his turn to give evidence, he has to be here. That is an important consideration. If he really wants to stay away because of his condition for the examination, the Trial Chamber will grant the application and there is no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we continue this morning, we agreed that, today, we continue the cross-examination of the second Defence witness for the first accused and it has so transpired that it is only the Prosecutor who has not started the cross-examination. Everyone else has started their cross-examination and merely reserved it for today. If you have to proceed with further cross-examination, you will cross-examine when the witness comes in. But, for the Prosecutor, he is starting his cross-examination. We will now start with those who have still reserved their cross-examination. Can we have the witness now, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the witness make his declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you are cross-examining. MUHAMED VEJZAGIC (continued) Cross-examined by MR. OLUJIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been in The Hague for quite some time. I believe that now we are winding down, I will be very short in asking you additional questions. May we start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, can we say that tempore criminis suspecti, that means the critical time frame that is between May and November 1992, in your view, according to your research and study, were there any ranks in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I did not hear whether the interpretation was completed. In this period, that is in 1992, from the outset of the war, there were no ranks in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Brigadier, again, based on your research, can you say that you could not find whether there were any rules -- house rules, that is, in the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My research did not find anything relating to those regulations with respect to the Celebici prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, since there were no ranks there, could we say that there was no special hierarchy in the prison, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through my research, I could not learn anything about the hierarchy within the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on your comprehensive experience and your study of this matter from the military point of view, based on that, can you say whether there were any rules that prevented members of the formations who were not part of the guard to enter Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My research also did not find any rules that would prevent such individuals from entering the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we also say that there was no way to prevent these persons from entering the prison if they did enter the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not establish any rules that the outsiders -- that would prevent the outsiders from entering the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MORAN (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the usher take the Brigadier volume III of his documents? (Handed). Brigadier, I would like you to look at one of the documents way in the back there -- it is document V-D/55. If it would help you, the Bosnian original is on page 859 and the first page of the English translation is on page 864. The document is the report of the commission appointed by the headquarters in Konjic to investigate the conditions in the Celebici camp. I just direct your attention to paragraph 2. It talks about the security team of 17 persons and the commander, who had that duty since 4 June 1992. Have we got the right document, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a document from 6 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct. I would direct your attention to paragraph 2 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this commission's report, other than just having seen it? Do you know anything at all about the commission's investigation -- any independent knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I only reviewed the roster of the guards and it also says that there is an order of the municipal commander -- I see it was Mirsad Catovic -- about receiving recruits -- I think it is his order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, on commission reports like this, are they sufficiently accurate, as a rule, that one can base factual determinations on the commission's report? So if, for instance, the commission reported that there was a security team of 17 people and named the commander, in all likelihood is that accurate information, given the way that these commissions operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where the problem is. I do not know what is in question -- I do not know what my answer should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you trying to find out whether the findings of the commission could be regarded as correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As accurate and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Can we regard the findings of this commission, that made this report, as accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not witness to these events, so I cannot speak to it, but if the commission made those findings, I guess they are probably fine, but I cannot determine anything in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, Brigadier. That is all I have and I thank you very much. Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have no further questions of this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours, please. Cross-examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I think your position is that you have no personal knowledge of the events that occurred in Konjic during the course of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot have personal knowledge of these events, because I was not an eye-witness, so my research is based on the documents and on my expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of preparing your statement, did you have access to any witness statements that you took into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which witnesses you have in mind -- I received certain statements from the Defence counsel, and, when preparing my report, I did speak to persons who were witnesses to the events with respect to some of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have access to any witness statements that have been provided by the Tribunal's Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What are you referring to -- persons detained in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please make it more clear to him. There were many witnesses not detained --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am asking a general question but I am primarily concentrating on those. I am interested generally in witness statements that you looked at, but, in particular, whether you had access to statements by people who had been detained -- can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to see such documents, which were shown to me by the Defence, and that focus on this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those statements that you saw, did any of them -- did you rely on any of them in order to form your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not rely on these statements, because they were not true, because my research has shown, by review of the documents, that there is quite a bit of untruth in these statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a record of the statements that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not keep any record of the review of these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said a moment ago that you also spoke to people in the area. Did you keep any record, tape recording, hand-written notes -- anything of that nature of the people that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have some personal notes with respect to the Celebici case. For instance, when I spoke to direct participants, like the chief of the municipal staff, I have notes on that; how certain things unfolded, things that I was interested in. I saw certain videotapes regarding the situation in Konjic, and that is about all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to people and where you took notes such as with the chief of the municipal staff, did you rely on those notes when you formed your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, I focused on documents, regardless of what people were saying -- the documents were really the true basis of my views that I formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we really explain this a little? You say the -- counsel is not saying you relied entirely on those things. They did assist you -- did those statements assist you in making up your opinion -- this is what he wants to know, not necessarily that you relied entirely on these statements -- whether they assisted you in making up your mind about the views you took.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were of assistance in general terms of forming my opinions. When you talk to some participant, it helps to clarify the situation, even though people do see people in different ways, so it is subjective views that you are encountering, but my basis for my expert's report were the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, you did not include any of these notes in your binder of material -- that is obvious; they are not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the notes as such I did not include.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the statements provided to you by the Defence as opposed to those that you may have seen from the Office of the Prosecutor, did you rely on those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reviewed those statements, but this was -- this came in quite late during my work on this expert's report, so when I arrived here, I saw that there were additional documents and there was some truth in them, but there was some untruth there as well. Based on what I found out in the documents, I saw that these statements were biased and so they were not supported by the documents which I had already included in my report, so I found no need to include them in my findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just turning to the documents themselves, did you include all the documents in your binders that you relied on in order to form your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I included such documents that I found of relevance, which confirm the state of affairs that I saw, but there was a whole mass of documents there, so there was no need to include all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find any documents that contradicted the point of view that you espoused in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have in mind the statements which I had an opportunity to see later on, and these were statements without proper seal or signature --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am not referring to statements; I am referring to documents. Did you find any documents amongst the material that you had which contradicted the point of view that you were espousing in your report -- documents, not statements? I have moved on to documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not find such documents which would point to any contradiction with respect to any particular document, that is, that it did not agree with that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to categorise for me the sources you relied on in order to obtain these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in my introduction, when I was asked by the Defence what were the sources of my knowledge, I said that they were documents which were at the disposal of the Institute; secondly, they were documents which the general staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had in their possession and documents that I found in the municipal staff -- municipal headquarters. Other various publications were also used and all these documents formed the basic documents, which helped me to form my opinion and present my expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the sources was the Defence, though, was it not -- you were given documents by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the documents that you were given, especially those given to you by the Defence, did you carry out any evaluation of them in order to determine their reliability and authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What factors did you rely on for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I relied on the verisimilitude of the documents and what I was able to see earlier on and I looked over the documents of the Defence, I compared the documents in my quest to arrive at the truth. Some of these documents exist -- there are facts in some of these documents which state that the events actually occurred, whereas, in another portion of the documents they did not bear out the facts and the document did not reflect the truth as I found it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, I now want to ask you some questions about your report itself. It is not necessary for you to go to each part of the report that I go to, unless you wish to, but I think you should have access to it just in case you do need it. Might the report be given to the Brigadier, please? (Handed). As I say, you do not have to go to each part, because I assume you know the contents of your report, so it is not necessary to look at it, but, if you want to, please feel free to do so. Professor, in the introductory part of your report, you say at page 1: "The JNA was a mutual armed force of all nations and nationalities in Yugoslavia and it constituted all branches of the service." I think you would agree with me the three main nationalities in Yugoslavia during the operation of the JNA were Serb, Croat and Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand -- how do you mean these three nations were in conflict?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not say anything about conflict. I just merely asked you whether -- I will be more specific -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time the three main nations represented were the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims -- you would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they are the nations that you are referring to when you say the JNA was a force that represented them -- initially, not at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not want you to reduce the problem to Bosnia -- we are talking about Yugoslavia, and then, afterwards, we can talk about Bosnia. There are other problems. You are speaking about the JNA. I do not know whether you have in mind the initial stages of the war in Slovenia and Croatia, but you are bringing me down to the problem in Bosnia. What do you want me to answer -- what question exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it would be easier if you answered the question asked. It is a straightforward one. These were the main entities in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Further on in your report at page 3 you speak of how the Territorial Defence was weakened by the withdrawal of arms and other military equipment -- this is on page 3. I take it that you are not suggesting, are you, that the decision to remove the arms from the Territorial Defence, which occurred under the direction of the SFRY, that there was anything illegal in that at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a completely legal decision of the military and political peaks in Belgrade -- it was not unlawful, illegal, at all. There was an order issued by the Federal Secretariat to withdraw the arms from the Territorial Defence units. It was stated that the arms would be looked after better and that they would be separated from the depot and that it be placed under army command in army depots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you say that this decision to remove the arms and ammunition from the TO did not occur in areas or regions that were predominantly inhabited by the Serb population; that is correct, is it not? You say that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say in my report that, in the areas where the Serb population lived, that arms were withdrawn later on, so where the population -- Serb population lived, the region was more secure and the arms were withdrawn to the army depots later on, but now we are dealing with the start of the whole conflict situation, there were army warehouses, army depots, and where it was considered unsafe to house ammunition and weapons, the weapons were removed and then they were returned to the area where the Serb population was predominant, whereas, later on, the arms were withdrawn completely, both where the Serbs lived and in other areas where there was a different population and immediately before the war, then the warehouses, which were located in areas where the Serb population was not the dominant population, from these warehouses material would be removed to the areas in Podrinje, Romanija and Sokolac, where there was a predominantly Serb population and those arms were later removed to these localities regardless of the fact they were army depots, because there was the danger that, in future operations, this would not be a safe place for the weaponry, so the arms were removed to what was considered safer localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 4 of your report you refer to the Ram Plan. In fact, I think you refer to it in a couple of places in your report. When you were in the JNA or at any other stage, indeed, did you ever have occasion to see the Ram Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the Ram Plan and I do not think anybody saw it, and that is standard practice, to use this term -- "the Ram Plan" -- it is standard terminology. I can only speculate when I say this, but it was the realisation, the implementation of a plan on the part of the Serb leadership to have the Virovitica, Karlobad, Karlovac Greater Serb territory formed, but I did not personally see the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met anyone who has?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 8 of your report, you speak there of the withdrawal of the JNA forces from Croatia, and you speak of them being placed in various regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In particular, you say the Maribor Corps was located in Banja Luka, Tuzla and Zenica. What source did you rely on for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the war, we had a lot of information, that is one source of the information and intelligence we received, but there is a report of February 1998, that is, it is a journal called "Hrvatske Vojnik", "Croatian Soldier", it is a publication put out in Croatia, and an admiral writes about this situation and about the war in Croatia and preparations for the war in Bosnia, and that is where that piece of information is contained. I have brought it with me -- I can show you -- and the author speaks in greater detail on the removal of the 14th Lubanje and 31st Maribor Corps and the 13th Rijeka Corps. This, for the most part, agrees with what I stated. He gives additional, more precise data, but the source is our knowledge before the war, in the course of the war -- before the war broke out in Bosnia, the intelligence service, as far as I was able, I came by this data and information and when a corps comes to a certain locality, we know what forces were sent where, so that the corps is not a small unit -- it is a vast unit and we saw that they were forces distributed along those localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you, Brigadier, that the 31st Maribor Corps was in fact moved to Jakovo, which is 10 kilometres west of Belgrade, you would disagree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How many kilometres did you say from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 10 kilometres west of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jakavo is far off from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I might have the distance wrong but if I were to suggest it was moved to Jakovo, you would disagree with that, too, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jakovo is Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Air Force Corps, which covered the 5th military region, was withdrawn to Bihac. Was that the 5th or the 10th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 10th Corps was the corps of the ground forces, the 5th is the Air Force Corps. This is an enormous difference, because the Air Force Corps covered the whole of the territory of Slovenia and Croatia and it was removed to Bihac in part and Banja Luka and to Glamoc in part where the airports exist. The difference is enormous. The 10th Zagreb Corps was a corps of the ground forces and the 5th is the Aviation Corps, the Air Force Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, further on in your report at page 12 you make reference to the fact that people were illegally carrying weapons and you refer us to the Resolutions by the Security Council in May 1992, so about this period of time I am referring to. Is your position that, so far as you understand it, that carrying of arms without a permit was illegal at the relevant time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Resolution 572 of the Security Council came somewhat later. I do not know where I said about the illegal carrying of arms. Who carried arms illegally? I am not sure what this is about -- do you mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify that, because it was a bit confusing. You say in your report that people who were arrested and taken to Celebici camp, a large number of them were arrested for illegally carrying arms; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that illegality arises because they did not have a permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not have a permit for this kind of weaponry -- permits were given for ordinary hunting arms, whereas a permit for army weaponry of a military type was not issued -- and nobody could come by such a permit. Permits are not issued for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An exception to this was, though, if you were a member of the armed forces -- you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the legal armed forces, of a recognised country, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the armed forces that were illegal or paramilitary, they illegally possessed weapons, if they had them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Paramilitary units which were not in the system, which were outside the Territorial Defence or the army, which came after 15 April, everything that was outside that system were considered to be paramilitary and illegal formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that military forces of other countries present in Bosnia at the time were illegally in possession of arms as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what military forces of Bosnia you have in mind. Were they forces who were in Croatia in the war or whether they were forces who fought against the JNA on the territory -- the JNA were the legal forces of the State in question, if that is your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you a general question. I am saying that forces of other countries that possessed weapons would have done so illegally at the relevant time, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Bosnia, as an internationally recognised country, foreign forces were the JNA forces and the forces of Croatia, they were also the forces of that particular country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, if, for example, the Novi Sad Corps was in Bosnia possessing weapons and carrying on military activity, you would regard that as illegal, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would consider this an aggression against Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, likewise, if Croatia had its forces there, that would be illegal as well, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the agreement. If the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina asked assistance from Croatia, then this would not be illegal. It would be an alliance and assistance in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would have been contrary to Resolution number 752, would it not, of 15 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that date on, when Resolution 752 came into being, all foreign forces were duty bound to withdraw from Bosnia, and they would then be considered illegal -- they could not remain in Bosnia as of that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be irrespective of any agreement that Bosnia may have entered into, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards agreements of this kind were formed, where joint action was required against the aggressor. At the time Croatian forces, like the Yugoslavia forces, were to have been guided by Resolution 752 and were to have withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or to come under the authority of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that was the other option for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If assistance is required and if the Government complies, then the forces would remain as allies in the operations, then this would be legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at no stage that happened, did it, Brigadier, that the Croatian forces or the forces of Serbia came under the authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the continued presence of Croatian forces and forces of Serbia, after 15 May 1992, would have been positively illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it should have been like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been the position for the HVO as well, was it not -- it was a force that did not come under the authority of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not the case with the HVO. The HVO was considered an armed force of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the later obstructions, regardless of the fact that they did not accept a unified command -- united command, but the HVO defended Bosnia-Herzegovina from the rebellious Serbs or "Chetniks", as they are called. We had brigades of the HVO along Majevica, the 111th and then the 110th unit, the Brcko 108th unit, so up to the conflict of January 1993 -- no, 9 May 1993, the forces of the HVO were a component part of the defence armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, they were not a foreign military force, they were considered to be legal armed forces defending Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, Brigadier, that the self-organised groups of citizens, at the beginning of the war, some of them did not come under the control of the legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that lasted well into 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think I could agree with that. We did have, in the course of the war, at the beginning of the war, self-organised groups of citizens under different terms. They were known by different names, but with the law on armed forces that was enacted, they were all placed under the system, so that the forces which were placed under the Patriotic League of the Green Berets and other names as well as the HVO and within them, the HOS units, all of them became part of the system on 15 April, so there is no question of 1993. We formed corps -- from October to December, we formed corps, and not some kind of groups working outside the system -- not at all. The rechannelling of the army went slowly -- it was a slow process and the first groups did exist in April, self-organised groups of citizens. For the most people, the people who were patriotically disposed, their initial arming was ad hoc, they used what they could find, hunting weapons and so on, and very quickly this became a problem, the force became larger, battalions and companies and detachments were being formed, which became the armed force and were led by commanders and in May the brigades were formed, so there were no self-appointed groups after May 1992, let alone 1993 when there was heavy fighting and when the commands of the corps were in charge of the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, from that, do I take it that it is your opinion that, at least after May 1992, there were no independent units operating in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There should not have been, apart from the fact that the forces of the Croatian defence force always had their directives from Grude, the headquarters in Grude and they were given their orders from Grude. Formerly they were in the composition of our form, for example the 111th, 108th, 110th, they all had the names of the HVO brigades but were part and parcel of the 2nd Corps. However, when our inspection went on the locality, I went to see whether the orders from the 2nd Corps reached the brigades and whether they were given tasks and we learnt that the directives came from the staffs in Grude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you what the position should have been, I am asking you what the position actually was. You mentioned the arms embargo having an impact on the ability of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina being able to arm itself for the conflict in 1992. By that, and accepting, and I accept, that there will no doubt have been considerable constraints upon the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of this embargo, but you are not suggesting, are you, that it was not breached from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arms embargo, for the most part, was directed at the Bosnian armed forces. I am not going to say this in absolute terms, but both the Serbs and Croats had the free flow of the arms. Had the embargo been lifted in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there would be much less destruction. It was very clear -- Yugoslavia was the fourth largest armed force in Europe. I am not going to say that there were illegal deliveries of arms. You cannot be allowed to just get slaughtered and not respond to that, so people probably used different channels and probably even bought arms from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And probably bought some from the Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also possible. Again, I have problems with the interpretation. It is alright now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you spoke about the fact that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a number of different groups which were finally put together at the end of the day into what became the corps. Your position, is it not, is that what is the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not really formally take shape and finally take shape until the corps were actually established at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forces of the Bosnian army developed from small groups of citizens and then very, very soon the youth of Bosnia responded to the call of arms, mostly Bosniaks and then also some Croats and Serbs, even, and so the army grew. However, you had a problem with personnel, the officers' corps, those who were going to organise and then train and lead the operations. As of May we had brigades established. When a corps gets 25 brigades, we had big communication problems, because you could not have 25 communication lines. If you issue an order to one brigade, you had to have 25 different brigades, so we had to enlarge these brigades, so we formed corps, we skipped divisions. So the corps were established in -- started being established in October and then, later, in November, and through reorganisation there were 6th and 7th Corps established, so from the brigades we move on to corps and the objective was efficiency in leading and controlling the units. Because the general staff, that is, the staff of the supreme command at first had to deal with about 90 brigades, and you know what kind of a task it is to command and control that many units, so we had to bring them together into larger formations so that we would be able to better command and control them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, in May and June of 1992, there were many parts of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were not even part of brigades or groups -- that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some parts, there were detachments that were left. However, in May and June, the brigades were developed, but it is a development -- it is something that you cannot rush, so it was an ongoing process throughout 1992. So, for instance, the 4th Corps was established in November 1992, so this was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we look at the outset, in April and May 1992, we have a situation such as this, do we not and I am talking about what became the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina: we had a fledgling military force, we had very few armaments, it lacked professional officers, its ultimate headquarters in Sarajevo were under attack, and the communications to its disparate parts throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina -- it is true, is it not, that the higher command in Sarajevo was so preoccupied with the siege that it was difficult to keep track of what was happening in regions such as Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Konjic was a specific case as well as Jablanica and other municipalities who used to be under the district staff in Mostar. Since there were differences in opinion with the HVO, this staff was not functioning and in those two headquarters, in Konjic and Jablanica, in the Neretva River valley were directly linked to the supreme command in Sarajevo, which was not the case with the others, who were linked to the district staffs in Tuzla, Sarajevo, Bihac, in Donje Gorazde and so forth. These two staffs were an exception as well as the municipal staff in Livno, which could never take hold, because the HVO forces were there, so those parts in -- so these municipal staffs were directly linked to the main staff in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you are disagreeing with me then when I say that communications between Konjic and Sarajevo were disrupted by the war and very difficult at the time -- you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said. At first, the communications in April were possible. However, later, there were major difficulties there. We could only send couriers and sometimes by radio communication. There were no protected communication lines. We did not have the equipment, we did not have the modern equipment in that regard, so that was a major problem -- a lack of communication lines, a lack of equipment -- so that the communication of the main staff with particularly small staff was very difficult and sometimes it took days for an order or a despatch to reach the subordinate to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, there was an issue, was there not, for Sarajevo, as to who in fact and indeed would be loyal to Sarajevo at the time in terms of persons selected to take command and control in remote regions -- regions remote from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what your question refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know whether I can make it much clearer. All I am saying is that, when it came to the selection of staff to control the military forces in remote regions, one of the issues that needed to be paid attention to in Sarajevo was the correct selection of people who at the time would be loyal to the cause of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- you do not disagree with that, surely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (INAUDIBLE).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: ... problem of disloyalty on the part of the local leaders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if the question referred to the loyalty of the local commanders -- I do not know if I ever addressed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It certainly, because of all these difficulties with communication and so forth, and the fact that the army was being established and developed, a great deal of responsibility was thrust upon, by necessity, the municipal authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army was not authorised to order anything to the municipal authorities -- the municipal authorities followed the laws that are their own and the army structures do not issue commands to them and do not control them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not answering my question, but the point I am making is that, because of these difficulties on the ground in Konjic, and on the ground in Sarajevo at the time, the municipality had to perform a much more significant role than would be the case if, for example, the JNA were still loyal and were still commanding the forces from an invasion from, say, an outside country outside of Yugoslavia, or do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not. As far as difference is concerned, in terms of authority, there are laws governing that and, in that sense, there is no difference whether there was an Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army structures of the JNA. That means the authorities do not step out of their competencies. The army has its own clearly defined duties and so do the authorities, regardless of whether it is the army or the TO that is in question. The authorities have their own set of rules that they follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no question about that, but the point I am putting to you, and -- I withdraw that. Are you suggesting that, on the ground -- and I am not talking about the pure science of the law, but are you suggesting the municipal authorities at no stage ever went beyond the reach of their legal authority -- is that your position, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are talking about the units and their use in combat, they never overstepped their authorities, but the truth is that they could do other things for the army, especially as far as logistics is concerned, providing food, clothing, et cetera. But the authorities do not meddle in the command and control -- they do not order the use of units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to the SDS, which you also speak about in your report at page 16, I am right, am I not, in saying that the position of the SDS in broad terms in 1992 was that, if Bosnia was not to remain part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then the Serb occupied or dominated part of Bosnia would be incorporated into a concept of Greater Serbia -- you would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And conversely the Muslim and Croat population saw themselves as being -- I withdraw that -- that the Croat population saw themselves as being distinct from the concept of Greater Serbia and so did the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the referendum of 29 March and 29 February and 1 March 1990, the elections were held, and the choice was whether to remain in Yugoslavia or not and the majority of Muslims, that is, Bosniaks, and Croats, I think 63 per cent or 64 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted that Bosnia should not remain within the former Yugoslavia. At that time, the concept that the Croats had was such that there was no difference between Croats and Bosniaks at that time -- Serbs had a different idea and a different political position which was dictated from Belgrade that Bosnia can only remain within Yugoslavia, and I would not go on to elaborate on this political issue -- I am a military expert, so please let us stay out of politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have already done so much, instead of answering "Yes" or "No" -- that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, on page 17 of your report, you make reference there to a place called Ostrozac, which you say is located in the immediate vicinity of Celebici, and you say none of the Serbs of this town were arrested or punished in any way. What is your source for that -- where did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Celebici, which at the request of the police surrendered their arms, were not arrested and they were all issued certificates of temporary requisition of their weapons and nobody touched them and nobody arrested them. This is a fact and this record still exists -- it is kept in Jablanica in the police headquarters, and you can verify it there, because it is in the control of the Jablanica authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is the source statement that none of them were arrested -- that is what I was interested in -- how did you know that none of them were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a conversation with a witness who was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a copy of that conversation, or did you make a note of the conversation, I should say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take any notes -- I thought that the conversation was enough, but I found that, as far as Ostrovac is concerned, this is what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this witness; who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a man who was questioning persons and who was issuing the certificates on temporary requisition of arms, so he was a member of the security authorities in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have his name there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you could rely on him as a source of that information. He has told you it was somebody who he interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We might like to know who it is, because we might like to speak to him ourselves, your Honour. He has not told us who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it your case that all the Serbs from that village left the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness says that none of them were arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, but if they are still there -- none of them were in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He said none of them were arrested or punished in any way. We are asking him how he found that out and who told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It could even be information which he can always remember -- what he thinks happened to a whole community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is in his report, it is tendered in evidence. I do not know what your Honours make of it that he cannot tell us who it was who told him. Perhaps you might look for it and tell us later, Brigadier. On page 17 of your report you speak of the fact that the SDS paramilitary formations in Borci took hostages of the then Konjic municipal president, the municipal executive board, and arrived for political negotiations. This issue of the SDS paramilitary taking hostages, where did you find that out from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a well known fact -- they went for negotiations there and were arrested, because they asked that the Serbs move out of Konjic and, if you allow people to leave, they would let them out of Konjic. The official policy was not to -- for the Serbs to stay in Konjic, not to move out, but the authorities that were already established in Borci asked that the Serbs move out. It was not difficult to find out why they wanted this, so that later they could shell, they could destroy Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand all of that, but it was not my question. I wanted to know who told you that, or how you found that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: One of your own witnesses spoke about Asim Dzambasovic being taken as a prisoner by the Serbs and then he entered into some sort of a compromise, which is not in the interests of the municipality -- one of your own witnesses spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know. I am asking did he speak to that witness. It is just a question. He writes a report, he gives us some of the material and not all of it. Surely I am allowed to pursue where he got his information from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not speaking for him, because some of these things are matters of common knowledge about the period at that time -- things which everybody else knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I am the only one who is not in that loop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have a look at your own witness statement then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I certainly am aware of the knowledge but not common, your Honours. On page 19 of your report you speak of the fact that the Igman military factory surrendered -- expressed its readiness to surrender to the legal authorities and so forth, so that those forces handed over the factory to the forces representing the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was there anyone arrested or anyone interrogated at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of hospital you are mentioning -- was this a hospital or a factory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A factory. I did not mention hospital at all -- the Igman military factory of ammunition and other products at page 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we received the translation of "hospital", which is why the witness is now confused. I see in the transcript it states "factory".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no fighting around the factory -- it was agreed that these were all workers, that there was no problem there. I do not know if anybody was arrested there, I do not have such information, but I know that the legal authorities took control of this facility and I know that a large quantity of weapons was taken then, but I do not know whether anybody was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if I were to suggest to you that at least one person was, you would not or could not disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not in a position to agree -- I was not a witness there, I am here under oath and so I can only confirm things that I know and I cannot agree to things that I am not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, paragraph number 2 on page 19, you speak of the taking of the Celebici facility and you say that the action of seizing the Celebici facility was managed by the then executive officer of the municipal Territorial Defence headquarters, Midhat Cerovac, the JNA soldiers found in the barracks safely left Konjic. I am not disputing that that may have happened. I am asking you what was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source of information was Cerovac, the commander, the chief of command, who was a witness there. There was no fighting there -- there was an agreement with the non-commissioned officer who was there in charge, he had about 20 to 30 soldiers there, they had negotiations which were political in nature, and he agreed to surrender without fighting, he feared that somebody would get injured and hurt, and so there was no fighting, and so they peacefully came in, and they collected whatever was there, some 20 or 30 pieces of small arms, and there were some hand-held rocket-propelled grenades and then they were released and they went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just really wanted to know who it was who told you and you did, you told us it was Cerovac. I have a simple question -- did you keep a record or note of the conversation you had with him about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have notes -- personal notes of my conversations with all individuals with whom I spoke. You cannot keep all that in your head -- it is a lot of material -- two months of research, so obviously I did keep notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Cerovac at the time was the executive officer of the municipal Territorial Defence headquarters -- what is that -- what is an "executive officer"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not executive -- you have commander and you have a chief, so he was person number 2 in the command. The commander commands and the chief is his deputy, and also coordinates everything and he usually proposes a decision to the commander, so there is no executive person, as you call it and the chief is not able to issue commands unless authorised by the commander to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will have to stop here. We will reassemble at noon. (11.30am) (A short break) (12.04pm) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Tell the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, we were discussing that part of your report where you speak of the taking over by the Territorial Defence of the Celebici barracks and you mentioned that a group was led by Midhat Cerovac. Do you know who was the commander of the Territorial Defence at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not -- there was not a commander -- he was chief of the staff. Cerovac was never commander of the municipal staff. This notion of commander of Territorial Defence does not exist -- it is commander of the staff -- commander of the municipal staff was somebody else and he was the chief in command --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the commander of the municipal staff then, that person, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, the commander of the municipal staff was it Omer Boric or perhaps -- I am not sure of the other name -- Omer Boric was ill for a time and had to leave for a time -- perhaps it was somebody else -- Ramic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been told or did you read anywhere a suggestion that the accused, Mr. Delalic, led the take-over of the Celebici facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delalic never is mentioned in any document as a military commander, except the time when he was commander of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not my question. My question is: had you read or have you been told at any stage that the accused Mr. Delalic led the take-over of the Celebici facility -- I did not ask you whether he was a military commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a statement, I seem to recall having read in a statement that Delalic led the group for taking over the Celebici facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, before I was asking you some questions about the 31st Corps in Maribor and I put it to you that it had been moved to a place 10 kilometres west of Belgrade and the place that I referred to was Jakovo and I think you told me that was in Croatia. Could you please look at the map that I now show you. I have extra copies for your Honours. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it really important to the case, the position of the 31st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is important to determine the accuracy and reliability of the report and to correct something that has been arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, just looking at that map there that is in front of you -- might this be given the next number in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Prosecutor Exhibit 219.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think if we place it on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is merely a map of the Belgrade area. (Handed). If you place it on the overhead protector, we can all see it then. Would you look at the machine beside you closely, please, Brigadier? Would you look at Belgrade, where you see "Belgrade" written on the map. Would you go directly west of Belgrade, about one centimetre. You need to look at the map as it appears on the screen -- it may be difficult to see on the projector. Do you see what I am pointing to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the airport of Sucin. If you are talking about west of Belgrade, 1 kilometre west, I do not know the scale of this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you go immediately below the airport of Sucin, do you see the name that appears immediately below it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says Jakovo -- that is a village -- the village of Jakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that that is where the 31st Maribor Corps was moved when the forces were taken from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the orders from the Federal Secretariat, these two corps were to have been deployed to Serbia, but, after the loss of the 17th Tuzla Corps in Slavonia, this corps was to have filled the gap of the 7th Tuzla Corps, so that this one corps did not remain in Serbia; it went to replace the Tuzla Corps, which was sent to fight in Slavonia and the 11th Corps was sent to Serbia -- when the 17th Corps sustained losses due to the fighting in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that map, your Honours. Brigadier, on page 23 of your report, you speak of a period in mid April 1992 and you say, "as the representative of the Republic of TO headquarters in mid April Lieutenant-Colonel Asim Dzambasovic arrived in Konjic". My question is, is this a gentleman that you spoke to and obtained a statement from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. His name is Asim Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This statement was not included in your materials, although it appears to be something that you relied upon -- where is the statement now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not draw up the report in writing, but just took the knowledge that he was -- that he came from Visoko, the region of Konjic, and he brought material with him concerning the organisation of the defence forces in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an expert opinion you are expressing, or are you just reciting what he has already told you as part of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is an officer with the command staff in the academy and there is no reason why I should doubt his knowledge. He is an expert officer, as I myself am, he knows the orders he received and what he did. There was no need for me to ask for a statement from him. We just had a talk and I was told what I was told -- the orders he had and how he translated them into practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, also on page 23 under the heading of the, "Organisation of the Municipal TO Headquarters", the first paragraph, you speak of the fact that the TO headquarters chief of staff was the second person in the line of authority and he at the same time held the position or had the duty of deputy commander. In relation to this part of your report, firstly, can you explain the different positions -- what do they normally entail, that is, the chief of staff and the deputy commander -- what is the difference between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we are only talking about that particular matter, then, in the former Yugoslavia, there was the notion of the commander -- the commander is the individual who decides, who takes decisions and it is only one individual who can take decisions -- that is one of the principles of command. The chief of headquarters staff is a different individual, and he is also the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is merely a question, Brigadier -- I am only asking you to tell me what the significance is of having two titles -- chief of staff and deputy commander and is there any difference between the roles performed by the deputy commander vis-à-vis the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it is one individual -- there is no deputy -- it is the chief of staff who is also deputy commander. When the commander is not there, he acts as deputy and the chief of staff in relation to the commander has quite a different function. The commander decides and the chief of staff decides on these decisions and takes part in the decision-making and it is the chief of staff that has all the information on one's own forces and on the basis of an analysis, an assessment, and appraisal, the commander brings in a decision when everybody sends in their reports to the chief of staff, who then puts forward a decision to the commander for the use of forces. The chief of staff does not decide on this particular matter. He can give a different decision if, according to his assessments and his knowledge, these do not coincide, and then he makes his decision regardless of the fact that the chief of staff has proposed a different decision -- he can reject the decision in part, or he can accept it as a whole. So when you are talking about the role of the chief of staff and the difference between the deputy commander, there is only a deputy when the commander himself is not there in person, and when he is authorised to take his place -- authorised the deputy to take his place, but this does not rid him of the responsibility for the repercussions of what he has conveyed to the commander, so it is always the commander who is responsible for the state of affairs in the units and the repercussions and everything that follows a given order or decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On page 25, you talk about the fact that, on 20 April 1992, the Celebici facility also held a station, Ministry of Interior units --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise to my colleague, but could he tell us the page in the Bosnian text? I see there is a significant difference -- the witness is losing time in finding the relevant passage, so could you give us the page in the Bosnian text, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would be delighted but I have never been given a copy of the Bosnian text. Even if I had been, I could not read it anyway, but I have never received a copy of it. I am afraid I am stuck with the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is fairly difficult to do that in practice except when you have had enough time to compare. Hopefully, we will follow it as it is, because I think the witness follows the Bosnian drafts while the Prosecutor is following the English draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is subheading (e) --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I will raise a matter with the Brigadier which may solve the problem anyway. I am asking you questions about your report, and I am really proceeding on an assumption that the questions I am putting to you are things that you know about, because you have written about them in the report. In fairness to you, I have an English version and you have a Bosniak version, and as best we try, interpretations may not always be accurate. So, when I put things to you, it may be that, relying upon the English version, I am not being precise so far as what you wrote in Bosniak. Please do not hesitate to say to me if you are confused or you think that I am not putting it correctly, because I do not want to be unfair to you -- I want to put it to you as fairly as possible and if what I am saying appears to be incorrect so far as what you intended, it could well be an interpretation error and I just invite you to do that. Moving on to page 25 of the report, it is under the heading "(e): Locations of the OSTO" et cetera and it is the fourth paragraph, there is a reference there to the HVO Splitska Brigade. Brigadier, the Splitska Brigade -- I take it that is a brigade that is named after the city of Split in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one would assume that it has been formed in the city of Split, that brigade; is that right, or am I wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming it had been formed in the city of Split, would it be a fair thing to say that it could be made up of people from Split -- maybe not entirely, but it could be made up of soldiers from the city of Split, or that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to wait so that I can find my own text. I cannot find this in my text on my page here. May I just have a few minutes to find it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring to paragraphs, I do not have paragraphs here. I do not know what you have in your translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is under part 4, which is the Konjic defence forces, and it is subparagraph (e) entitled "Location of the OSTO and the Deployment of Units" and it is about 10 lines -- 14 lines more precisely in English down from the top --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I may be able to help. I am informed it is page 31 of the Bosnian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Page 31, thank you, I am indebted to my learned friend. Page 31?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my page 31 I cannot find it. What is written there is on the command and the combat units and the areas in which they were active, the Celebici facility of 20 April with the MUP units, so it does not seem to me to be on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is that particular part you are reading now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Split Brigade, is that what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the forces of the Croatian defence forces with about 120 Croats, locally called the Split, Splitska Brigade. I cannot maintain for sure where the name came from. I am not a witness of the events -- whether they were actually people from Split or whether the local Croats just gave themselves the term of "Split".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Going over to page 27 of the English version, and it is the last section of paragraph (f), "Leadership and Command of the Territorial Units" and it is perhaps more easily found three paragraphs above the next major heading, "Ministry of Interior Police Forces as Part of the Konjic Defence". I wanted to ask you some questions there about a section of your report where you speak of the fact that the OSTO of the Bosnian army had supervision over lower commands and units and the word in English that I have is that "an anarchy was never a characteristic thing at any point over 1992". It is the word "anarchy" in English, whether that is the same word that you used, that is of interest to me. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you tell me the line -- we have page 32, six lines -- where do you find the word "anarchy"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I help? It is the one but last paragraph, the second but last paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure whether the word "anarchy" is the word selected by you or whether it was a word selected by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are talking about "anarchy" in the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is proof that, in the system of command, there was always the law of conduct within the rules and regulations for leadership and command, the principles on which this was based and it is maintained that there was never any anarchy, a state of anarchy in the system of control and command. There were principles governing the system of control and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that, are you saying that there were no cases at any stage of people taking independent action, or failing to obey orders in the Konjic area during that period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not a witness of the events in Konjic and the possibility that individuals sort of step out of the system cannot be excluded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may not have been a witness to the events, but you make a pretty clear statement there, that it was "never a characteristic thing" and that is the issue I am really addressing myself to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you say that there was no anarchy, that is a general statement -- that means within the system. But, you can never exclude the fact that sometimes within any army, any individuals can operate outside of the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I were to show to you a document by the TG1 commander of 30 October 1992, the accused, Mr. Delalic, complains of a failure to comply with an order, you would not say -- you would not deny that; you would simply say that it is not a matter that you intended to deal with when you used this expression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- it is probably some kind of order to the Tactical Group 1 that it was issued to a commander who did not carry it out. Maybe the order was not carried out in a timely fashion rather than the order was refused to be carried out. Those are two separate things -- one is not carrying it out timely and the other one is to refuse to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should show you the document so that we can deal with it. This is a document that has previously been given to the Defence but it is not an exhibit. I ask that it be marked with the exhibit number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 220.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, it is not a very good copy, so I hope that you are able to read it clearly enough (Handed). But in particular, do you see in the very first paragraph what appears to be there a complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot read the copy very well. I cannot see who is the author. You cannot see the headings -- I see that the date is 31 October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot see who signed this document and who issued this document -- there is no signature on it, so I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I suggest you look at the very bottom of the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no signature -- it says "Commander of TG1 Delalic", but there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You know, as a military man, that this is a telex, do you not, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the contents of this document, so I would need some time to study it in order to ascertain its authenticity. I cannot speak to it right now. So, I do not know where the problem is. He does not give the daily report -- I do not know if this is a failure to carry out an order or is this a refusal, so I would have to study it a bit closer in order to give you my expert military opinion. I cannot see any signature here, and up here I cannot see who is sending it, who the author is. Is this the Tactical Group that is sending it, in which case it should state there, and I can also not see the commander's signature. If this is the commander Zejnil Delalic, then there should be "SR" which stands for "in his own handwriting", so that we can trace the original document back, so I cannot say this is an authentic document, because I do not have any proof of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you seriously suggesting that as a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that if you received a telex message in the field, or wherever, which issued you with an order, you would refuse to obey it because it happened to be a telex -- are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What I say is that it has to state "commander" in his own handwriting, so "SR" would be the abbreviation and that is a statement that confirms that it was sent by who states on the document that they have sent it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that -- whether or not you would accept it yourself, you would agree with me that there is a suggestion in this that not all orders were being obeyed at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. Even though I worked in the general staff, the staff of the supreme command, I am not aware of the cases where orders were not carried out, so I am unaware of this case, even though I worked in the supreme command staff. I did not have an opportunity to study this document, so I cannot tell you in which sense the orders were not carried out. That is a very serious matter -- if that is determined, then you go and you are court-martialled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly you would not have carried out this. If this had been an order directed to you, I take it you would have just ignored it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not an order as far as I can see; this is a report. It is a report to a superior. If this was addressed to Zejnil -- that is, if this is Zejnil, then it was a report to Sefer, so it is a report on something, so I cannot comment on it now because I would have to read it first, so this is not an order -- this is a report of a subordinate to a superior and it is a report on the situation -- the state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will not waste any more time. Might that be marked for identification? On page 28 of your report, which is under the next heading 4.2, "Ministry of Interior Police Forces as Part of the Konjic Defence", you say that: "Given that in the beginning of the war the Territorial Defence did not have an organised military police, all arrests of persons in the illegal possession of arms, as well as arrests of persons deprived of liberty after the actions in Donje Selo and Bradina, were performed by the SJB Konjic Police Forces and by the HVO military police." Are you saying that the Territorial Defence, when it was engaged in military activity, carried out no arrests whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
